{{Short description|Concept in epidemiology}}
{{Orphan|date=October 2025}}

The '''Table 2 Fallacy''' is a term coined by Daniel Westreich and [[Sander Greenland]] in 2013.<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://academic.oup.com/aje/article/177/4/292/147738 |title = The Table 2 Fallacy: Presenting and Interpreting Confounder and Modifier Coefficients| date=2013 | doi=10.1093/aje/kws412 | last1=Westreich | first1=D. | last2=Greenland | first2=S. | journal=American Journal of Epidemiology | volume=177 | issue=4 | pages=292–298 | pmid=23371353 | pmc=3626058 }}</ref> It is a concept in [[causal inference]].{{citation needed|date=March 2025}}

In scientific papers reporting observational studies, people often report both crude and adjusted associations between variables included in a regression model and the outcome of interest in Table 2. If the purpose of the analysis is causal inference, usually, the variables one would choose to adjust for will differ for each exposure - outcome pairing. The Table 2 Fallacy occurs when people seek to give a causal interpretation to the other parameters estimated using a multivariable regression model that was only designed to explore a single exposure - outcome association.

Table 2 Fallacy is a common error made in reporting epidemiological results in a wide range of subject areas.<ref>{{cite journal |title = Revisiting the Table 2 Fallacy: A Motivating Example Examining Preeclampsia and Preterm Birth| date=2018 | pmc=6103824 | last1=Bandoli | first1=G. | last2=Palmsten | first2=K. | last3=Chambers | first3=C. D. | last4=Jelliffe-Pawlowski | first4=L. L. | last5=Baer | first5=R. J. | last6=Thompson | first6=C. A. | journal=Paediatric and Perinatal Epidemiology | volume=32 | issue=4 | pages=390–397 | doi=10.1111/ppe.12474 | pmid=29782045 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title = Interpreting mutual adjustment for multiple indicators of socioeconomic position without committing mutual adjustment fallacies| date=2019 | pmc=6319005 | last1=Green | first1=M. J. | last2=Popham | first2=F. | journal=BMC Public Health | volume=19 | issue=1 | page=10 | doi=10.1186/s12889-018-6364-y | doi-access=free | pmid=30606167 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/cdoe.12617 |title = A scoping review of Table 2 fallacy in the oral health literature| date=2021 | doi=10.1111/cdoe.12617 | last1=Akinkugbe | first1=Aderonke A. | last2=Simon | first2=Alyssa M. | last3=Brody | first3=Erica R. | journal=Community Dentistry and Oral Epidemiology | volume=49 | issue=2 | pages=103–109 | pmid=33368566 | url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1063458421007056 |title = Multivariable models in orthopaedic research: a methodological review of covariate selection and causal relationships |journal = Osteoarthritis and Cartilage |date = July 2021 |volume = 29 |issue = 7 |pages = 939–945 |doi = 10.1016/j.joca.2021.03.020 |last1 = Ponkilainen |first1 = V. A high profile example was a paper exploring associations between demographic and health characteristics and death from COVID-19,<ref>{{cite journal |title = Factors associated with COVID-19-related death using OpenSAFELY| date=2020 | doi=10.1038/s41586-020-2521-4 | last1=Williamson | first1=Elizabeth J. | last2=Walker | first2=Alex J. | last3=Bhaskaran | first3=Krishnan | last4=Bacon | first4=Seb | last5=Bates | first5=Chris | last6=Morton | first6=Caroline E. | last7=Curtis | first7=Helen J. | last8=Mehrkar | first8=Amir | last9=Evans | first9=David | last10=Inglesby | first10=Peter | last11=Cockburn | first11=Jonathan | last12=McDonald | first12=Helen I. | last13=MacKenna | first13=Brian | last14=Tomlinson | first14=Laurie | last15=Douglas | first15=Ian J. | last16=Rentsch | first16=Christopher T. | last17=Mathur | first17=Rohini | last18=Wong | first18=Angel Y.
